Discharge Summary
Service: General medicine

Chief Complaint: Lightheadedness when standing.

Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: None during this admission.

History of Present Illness:
The patient was admitted after becoming lightheaded on the way from the bedroom to the kitchen. The daughter saw the patient reach for the back of a chair and helped the patient sit down. There was no loss of consciousness, head strike or injury. The patient remembered the entire episode and described dimming of vision on standing, with prompt relief on sitting. There had been several days of loose stools and very little appetite. Small sips of tea stayed down, but the patient had stopped eating regular meals. There was no blood in the stool, abdominal pain or vomiting. The patient denied chest discomfort, palpitations and a sensation of the room spinning.

The daughter brought the medication organiser to the emergency department. It appeared that the patient had continued the usual morning tablets throughout the illness. In the emergency department the patient became symptomatic again while standing for blood pressure measurement. Symptoms eased after intravenous fluid. The patient remained unsteady walking to the bathroom and was admitted for further assessment of oral intake, renal function and mobility.

Past Medical History:
Hypertension, osteoarthritis of both knees and intermittent constipation. At baseline the patient uses a walking stick outside and can move between rooms at home without assistance. Knee pain makes it difficult to stand long enough to prepare a full meal.

Medications on Admission:
An oral antihypertensive, a thiazide diuretic, a bowel preparation used as needed for constipation and paracetamol for joint pain. The daughter confirmed that the bowel preparation had been put away when loose stools began.

Social History and Baseline Function:
The patient lives with an adult daughter in a flat with lift access. They share a kitchen and take their evening meal together. The daughter prepares meals, sets out the morning tablets and helps the patient get into the shower. The patient can dress independently once seated and manages toileting without help. The daughter described feeling overwhelmed by the amount of care needed alongside the ordinary household tasks. The patient would like to resume making breakfast independently so that the daughter can leave for work without waiting.

Asked about contact outside the home, the patient said that visits with friends stopped when knee pain made leaving the flat difficult. The daughter is the only person the patient sees in a typical week. The patient described feeling cut off from friends and would welcome a regular visitor. Money for food also runs short towards the end of the month. The patient sometimes skips lunch to leave enough groceries for the evening meal.

Physical Exam on Admission:
Alert and able to give a coherent account. Mouth dry. Pulse regular at rest, increasing on standing as the blood pressure fell and lightheadedness returned. Chest clear. Abdomen soft with mild diffuse discomfort on deep palpation and no guarding. Speech and limb movements symmetric. The patient could take a few steps with assistance but asked to sit before reaching the door.

Pertinent Results:
Admission blood work showed a rise in creatinine relative to the previous outpatient result and a mildly low potassium concentration. Haemoglobin was similar to baseline. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Repeat blood tests after oral intake resumed showed improving renal function and potassium within the laboratory reference range. No further loose stool was available for sampling on the ward.

Brief Hospital Course:
Volume depletion and near syncope. The history of gastrointestinal losses, reduced intake and symptoms reproduced on standing supported volume depletion. The diuretic was withheld and fluid was given while the patient was unable to drink comfortably. Nursing staff initially accompanied the patient out of bed. By the following morning the patient was drinking from a jug without prompting and ate part of breakfast. Fluids were discontinued. There was no recurrent diarrhoea, and the patient tolerated ordinary meals before discharge. Repeat standing measurements did not reproduce the presenting symptoms.

Mobility. At the first therapy assessment the patient used the arms of the chair to stand, then paused before taking a step. Knee stiffness persisted after the lightheadedness had resolved. With the usual walking stick the patient subsequently walked the length of the corridor and turned without losing balance. The therapist also observed a transfer from a low seat to approximate the chair used at home. The daughter confirmed that the distance from bed to bathroom was shorter than the distance walked on the ward.

Discharge planning. The social worker met the patient and daughter separately before a joint discussion. The patient agreed to a referral for grocery support and asked for details of a visiting service. The daughter requested information about occasional relief with personal care. She was able to continue the usual routine on return home but could not take on additional daytime visits. These requests were recorded for community follow-up. No new home service had started by the time of discharge.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Volume depletion with postural lightheadedness and transient kidney injury in the setting of a resolving diarrhoeal illness.

Discharge Condition and Disposition:
Eating, drinking and passing urine normally. Walked to the bathroom using the usual stick. Returned to the flat shared with the daughter.

Discharge Medications:
The discharge list distinguishes the regular blood pressure tablet from the diuretic that remains on hold. The daughter reviewed the list with the ward pharmacist and identified which tablet to leave out of the organiser pending reassessment.

Discharge Instructions and Follow-up:
The team discussed maintaining access to drinks during the day and sitting down if lightheadedness returns. The patient and daughter could describe the circumstances that would prompt reassessment, including fainting or inability to keep fluids down. Primary care follow-up was requested for a blood pressure check, repeat renal blood work and review of the diuretic. The discharge handover also records the patient's preference to be contacted directly about the visiting service.

Discharge Summary
Service: General medicine

Chief Complaint: Cough, wheeze and difficulty breathing.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had been well enough to do the usual shopping until a sore throat and dry cough developed. Over the next few days the cough began waking the patient from sleep. Walking from the sitting room to the front door brought on chest tightness and audible wheeze. The rescue inhaler gave brief relief, but the symptoms returned before the patient could finish dressing. A friend who was visiting for coffee suggested seeking assessment. The patient denied fainting, pain on inspiration, blood in the sputum or swelling of the legs. There was no recent change in bedding, cleaning products or smoking exposure.

In the emergency department the patient could describe the symptoms in short phrases and had widespread expiratory wheeze. Breathing was easier after inhaled treatment, although the patient still had to stop to catch breath on the way to the toilet. Admission was arranged because symptoms recurred with minimal exertion and the patient was having difficulty coordinating the inhaler while breathless.

Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: None.

Past Medical History:
Asthma with intermittent exacerbations and seasonal rhinitis. Between episodes the patient usually walks outdoors daily and can carry a small bag of groceries home. There is no baseline oxygen requirement. The patient recalled previous instruction in using a spacer but had put it away when symptoms settled.

Medications on Admission:
A maintenance inhaler and a separate reliever inhaler were brought in from home. The patient could distinguish them by appearance but was less sure of the names. The maintenance inhaler had been used irregularly when breathing felt comfortable. Also takes an antihistamine during symptomatic periods.

Social History:
The patient lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment and intends to return there after discharge. The patient reports having no caregiver and independently manages cooking, bathing, shopping and medication. A neighbour has a spare key for emergencies. Neither the neighbour nor the visiting friend provides regular help with personal care or household tasks.

The patient speaks with friends most days, plays cards with neighbours twice a week and usually joins a walking group. The patient denied feeling isolated and described having as much company as desired. The recent absence from the card game was due to coughing. The patient asked to make a call from the ward so that the group would know why the usual seat was empty. There is food in the apartment and the patient expects to prepare a simple meal on returning home. No current alcohol or tobacco use was reported.

Physical Exam:
On arrival the patient was seated upright, with prolonged expiration and wheeze audible throughout both lung fields. Air entry was present on both sides. No focal crackles. Heart rhythm regular. No calf tenderness or peripheral oedema. Alert and attentive, with normal speech once the initial breathlessness eased. Examination after inhaled treatment showed less effort at rest but persistent wheeze on a short walk.

Pertinent Results:
Chest radiograph showed no focal airspace opacity or pleural fluid. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Blood work did not suggest significant anaemia or a disturbance in renal function. Oxygen saturation remained satisfactory at rest. During the initial walk the patient stopped because of chest tightness despite preserved oxygen saturation. Subsequent walks were assessed using both symptoms and the distance tolerated.

Brief Hospital Course:
Asthma exacerbation. The patient received inhaled bronchodilator treatment and a short course of systemic corticosteroid. There was no focal examination or radiographic finding to suggest bacterial pneumonia. Cough persisted overnight but became less frequent, and the interval between reliever treatments increased. By the final ward round the patient had washed, dressed and eaten breakfast without pausing for breath. A walk along the corridor at the patient's usual pace produced mild cough without chest tightness. Supplemental oxygen was not required.

Inhaler review. During the first demonstration the patient released the spray before sealing the lips around the mouthpiece. The respiratory nurse demonstrated the spacer and asked the patient to repeat the sequence using a training device. On a second attempt the patient prepared the device correctly and took each inhalation separately. The pharmacist and patient agreed on plain-language labels for the maintenance and reliever inhalers. The patient chose to keep the spacer beside the maintenance inhaler at home and could explain when each device would be used.

Function and discharge planning. Staff observed independent transfers, dressing and walking once the acute wheeze had settled. The patient was comfortable going home and did not request help with daily activities. A friend offered a lift home and arranged to return for their usual coffee visit later in the week. The patient wished to resume the walking group when the cough allowed and planned to start with the shorter route used on previous occasions.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Acute asthma exacerbation following upper respiratory symptoms.

Discharge Medications:
Maintenance and reliever inhalers were reconciled with the devices the patient had brought in. The remaining corticosteroid course and its stop point were recorded on the discharge list. The patient packed the spacer with the inhalers before leaving the ward.

Discharge Condition:
Speaking comfortably in full sentences. Good bilateral air entry with slight wheeze on forced expiration. Independent with usual personal care.

Discharge Disposition: Returned to own apartment.

Discharge Instructions and Follow-up:
The patient reviewed the written inhaler plan with the nurse and identified persistent breathlessness at rest or diminishing relief from the reliever as reasons to seek urgent review. The primary care handover requests reassessment of symptoms, reliever use and inhaler technique after recovery. The patient will bring the devices and spacer to that appointment. A copy of the medication list was placed with the written plan at the patient's request.

Discharge Summary
Service: General medicine

Chief Complaint: Pain and redness around a scrape on the lower leg.

History of Present Illness:
The patient scraped the shin against the edge of a cupboard while putting groceries away. The skin break was small and initially caused little discomfort. Over the following days the surrounding skin became warm, and the sock on that side felt tight. The patient's partner noticed that the red area extended beyond the edge of the dressing when it was changed. Standing to cook became uncomfortable, although the patient could still move the ankle and bear weight. The patient reported poor sleep because of an aching sensation in the shin and came for assessment when elevation alone no longer brought relief.

There had been no bite, puncture wound or immersion injury. The patient did not describe shaking chills, drainage of pus or loss of sensation in the foot. On assessment the lower leg was swollen with redness centred around the abrasion. The margins were marked to help the team assess progression. The patient was admitted for antimicrobial treatment and assessment of mobility because the bathroom at home was some distance from the bedroom.

Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: None. No collection required drainage.

Past Medical History:
Chronic dependent ankle swelling and osteoarthritis affecting the hands. The ankle swelling usually improves overnight. Before this episode the patient was mobile indoors without a walking aid. Hand stiffness occasionally makes it difficult to open packets or secure a bandage, particularly first thing in the morning.

Medications on Admission:
A regular blood pressure tablet and an as-needed analgesic for joint discomfort. The patient and partner reviewed the home list together. No antimicrobial had been started before presentation.

Social History and Living Arrangements:
The patient and partner live together in a single-storey home. There is a shallow step at the entrance, and the bedroom and bathroom are on the same level. The patient usually does the cooking. Since the injury the partner has prepared meals, changed the leg dressing and helped the patient wash the affected leg. The partner expects to continue helping during recovery and denied feeling strained by these tasks. Both said there was enough food at home.

The patient described regular conversations with relatives and a weekly shared meal with friends. The patient enjoys these visits and feels well connected to the group. Leg pain caused the patient to miss the most recent meal, and friends have arranged to bring the next meal to the house. The partner usually spends part of the day outside the home. The patient can contact the partner if help is needed and is comfortable being alone for those intervals.

Physical Exam on Admission:
Alert, conversant and comfortable with the leg supported. A superficial abrasion was present over the shin, with surrounding warmth, tenderness and poorly demarcated erythema. No fluctuance, crepitus or pain on passive movement of the ankle. The foot was warm with intact sensation. The patient stood from a chair without assistance but shortened the step on the affected side. The opposite ankle had mild swelling without tenderness or redness.

Pertinent Results:
Initial blood work showed a mild inflammatory response with renal function near baseline. Ultrasound showed soft tissue swelling without a drainable collection. Venous imaging did not show an acute deep vein thrombosis in the affected leg. The white cell count trended down as the local symptoms improved. Further imaging was deferred because the patient regained comfortable weight bearing and the tenderness remained superficial.

Brief Hospital Course:
Lower leg cellulitis. Treatment began with an intravenous antibiotic and elevation of the affected leg. Early nursing reviews documented the position of the redness relative to the admission markings. By the next dressing change the skin was less tense, the tender area had receded and the patient could rest the foot on the floor without throbbing. The patient remained afebrile. Once improvement was sustained, treatment was changed to an oral antibiotic, which the patient tolerated with meals.

Wound care. The abrasion remained shallow with scant clear drainage. The wound nurse demonstrated removal of the dressing without pulling at the surrounding skin. Hand stiffness made it awkward for the patient to secure the replacement dressing. At the patient's request the partner attended the next change, arranged the supplies within reach and completed the dressing with the nurse observing. The partner could identify the edge of the residual redness and described which changes would prompt a call for reassessment. A small supply of dressings was arranged for home.

Mobility and function. Early in the admission the patient used a walking frame for comfort on the way to the bathroom. After the swelling subsided, the therapist observed the patient walk a similar distance without the frame and manage a low step using the rail. The patient could sit at the kitchen table to help prepare food while the partner continued the tasks that required prolonged standing. Both felt this arrangement would work in the existing home layout.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Cellulitis surrounding a superficial abrasion of the lower leg. Chronic dependent ankle swelling.

Discharge Condition and Disposition:
Pain controlled with oral medication. Small area of residual redness around a clean abrasion, without further extension. Returned to the home shared with the partner.

Discharge Medications:
Oral antibiotic to complete the prescribed course. The pharmacist went through the course end point with the patient and confirmed that the regular home tablet was listed correctly. The patient tolerated the oral medication before leaving.

Discharge Instructions and Follow-up:
The patient received the dressing plan and a request for outpatient wound review. Spreading redness, new drainage, fever or increasing difficulty bearing weight were discussed as reasons for earlier reassessment. The partner will help with dressing changes and accompany the patient to the first review. The handover asks the community clinician to reassess the abrasion and residual swelling and to review whether assistance with dressing changes is still needed as hand comfort and mobility allow.
